messages.subject: jacobian adjustment for squared_distance?
parts:
Greetings!

I put together a model that has 2 sets of parameters that I want to be similar unless the data suggests otherwise. I implemented this idea by using squared_distance. So I have parameter vector v1 and parameter vector v2. I take similarity = squared_distance(v1,v2) in the transformed parameters block and then sample similarity from exponential(1). When stan builds my model I get a warning:


DIAGNOSTIC(S) FROM PARSER:
Warning (non-fatal):
Left-hand side of sampling statement (~) may contain a non-linear transform of a parameter or local variable.
If it does, you need to include a target += statement with the log absolute determinant of the Jacobian of the transform.
Left-hand-side of sampling statement:
    similarity[lev, pa] ~ exponential(...)


I read through chapter 33 of the manual. I understood that I need to adjust the target by the absolute determinant of the jacobian of the transform. However, my jacobian isn't square. It's 1 by the number of parameters times 2. I didn't search exhaustively, but I didn't find this situation addressed in the manual. What is the proper thing to do?

Thank you.

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] jacobian adjustment for squared_distance?
parts:
Our Jacobians are the usual ones from multivariate
calculus change of variables. They are always N to N.

If you try to do this:

d(y1, y2) = (y1 - y2)' * (y1 - y2)

and then say

d(y1, y2) ~ foo(...)

you'll see that you can't properly normalize in the
2N-dimensional space making up y1 and y2 because you
can move y1 and y2 together in any direction to get the
same distance. This is why you need N to N transforms.
They need to map volumes to volumes or you wind up
with unmeasureable sets (too low a dimension). And it
needs to be an invertible mapping, which also won't work
with a reduction to distances.

But all is not lost. We encourage people to think of
models generatively, and it just so happens that least squares
wasn't an accident, and that:

log multi_normal(y1 | y2, I) = - 0.5 * d(y1, y2) + constant

So what you can do is put a conditional distribution on y1 given
y2 based on distance. Then you can put whatever distribution you
want on y2 and the result will be a well normalized prior if
the prior on y2 can be normalized. (Stan doesn't need the normalization
constants, but it does require posteriors to be proper.)

Alternatively, you may be thinking about something like both y1 and y2
coming from some process that generates them starting from some shared latent
z, in which case you can have something like:

p(y1 | z) = ...
p(y2 | z) = ...
p(z) = ...

But without something anchoring the position, you won't get a normalizable
prior.

- Bob

> Ah, that works!

Oh, and it's more efficient to code in Stan as

y1 ~ normal(y2, sigma);

assuming the length scale's the same in every dimension. Or even just
fix a value for sigma (I did that implicitly with I, which I should've
included as sigma * I, where I is the identity matrix).

- Bob
